question: Describe a time you had to present to senior leadership or a skeptical audience. How did you prepare and what was the result?

raiseTranscript.text: I presented my first feature launch metrics to my manager and one skip-level after a customer complained about a bug. I prepared by pulling the exact error logs, running a quick A/B test summary, and practicing the 5-slide deck with my mentor twice. I opened with the customer quote, showed the root cause in one chart, and ended with the fix timeline. They approved the hotfix that day.
What feedback did you get on your delivery?
My manager said the data was clear but I spoke too fast on the timeline. I slowed down in the next update and it landed better.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to present to senior leadership or a skeptical audience. How did you prepare and what was the result?

Role: new grad on small feature team; Situation: bug complaint after launch; Actions: pulled logs + A/B summary, practiced with mentor, 5 slides; Outcome: hotfix approved same day; Quote: "I slowed down in the next update and it landed better"; Follow-up: delivery feedback received and applied
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. Competency is Communication. The candidate described preparing a 5-slide deck on a feature bug by pulling logs and practicing with a mentor, then adjusting pace after direct feedback. This shows ownership of individual work and coachability. The concrete outcome was same-day hotfix approval. The story stays local but demonstrates learning in real time. Biggest strength is applying feedback on delivery without defensiveness.

lowerTranscript.text: I had to show my project status to the director once. I just copied the JIRA tickets into a doc and walked through them. They asked a lot of questions about risks and I didn't have the numbers ready so it went long.
How did you prepare for the questions?
I didn't really. I figured they would just want the status.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to present to senior leadership or a skeptical audience. How did you prepare and what was the result?

Role: individual contributor; Situation: director status update; Actions: copied JIRA into doc, no prep on risks; Outcome: meeting ran long with unanswered questions; Quote: "I figured they would just want the status"; Follow-up: no evidence of adjusting approach
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. Competency is Communication. The candidate copied JIRA tickets without anticipating questions and admitted they expected the audience to only want raw status. No preparation or follow-up adjustment shown. The result was an unfocused meeting. This misses the basic expectation that even junior roles own clear delivery to stakeholders. Biggest gap is lack of any visible learning or ownership of the outcome.

raiseTranscript.text: I needed buy-in from two other teams' tech leads to adopt a shared retry library. I built a one-pager with latency data from our service and theirs, ran a 2-week pilot, then presented to the three leads plus their managers. I opened with the cross-team p99 impact, showed the pilot results in a table, and proposed a 4-week rollout. Both teams agreed and we shipped it.
One lead worried about maintenance. I had already asked their on-call how many incidents they saw and included that number, which addressed it.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to present to senior leadership or a skeptical audience. How did you prepare and what was the result?

Role: senior on platform team; Situation: cross-team adoption of retry library; Actions: one-pager with latency data, 2-week pilot, included on-call incident count; Outcome: both teams agreed to 4-week rollout; Quote: "I had already asked their on-call how many incidents they saw"; Follow-up: addressed maintenance concern with pre-collected data
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. Competency is Communication. The candidate prepared a data-backed one-pager and pilot results to influence two peer teams without authority, directly addressing the maintenance concern with on-call numbers. The result was agreement on rollout. Story shows influence across teams with measurable prep. Biggest strength is anticipating skepticism and closing it with targeted evidence before the meeting.

lowerTranscript.text: I presented the new service design to the architecture review board. I walked through the diagrams I had in my design doc and answered questions as they came up. A couple of principals pushed on scalability and I said we could look at it later.
Did you follow up on the scalability concerns?
Not really, the meeting ended and the design was approved anyway.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to present to senior leadership or a skeptical audience. How did you prepare and what was the result?

Role: senior individual contributor; Situation: architecture review board; Actions: walked through existing diagrams; Outcome: approved but scalability questions deferred; Quote: "the design was approved anyway"; Follow-up: no follow-up on concerns raised
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. Competency is Communication. The candidate presented existing design diagrams to the architecture board and deferred scalability questions without resolution. Approval happened but no evidence of proactive influence or cross-team alignment. The story lacks the data prep or audience adaptation expected at senior level. Biggest gap is treating the skeptical audience as an obstacle rather than preparing to address their concerns.

raiseTranscript.text: My team had missed two quarters on a key initiative. I prepared a 15-minute update for the VP and directors that included team health metrics, the root causes I had identified with each engineer, and a revised plan with clear owners. I opened with the two-quarter miss, showed the per-person breakdown, then proposed moving one person to a different project. The VP approved the re-plan.
How did the team react to the change?
I had 1:1s with both engineers beforehand so they understood the rationale and the new scope.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to present to senior leadership or a skeptical audience. How did you prepare and what was the result?

Role: engineering manager; Situation: two-quarter miss on initiative; Actions: team health metrics, root causes from 1:1s, proposed reallocation; Outcome: VP approved re-plan; Quote: "I had 1:1s with both engineers beforehand"; Follow-up: pre-socialized change with affected team members
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. Competency is Communication. The candidate prepared a metrics-driven update on a missed initiative, included individual root causes, and pre-communicated a staffing change before the VP meeting. Result was approval of the revised plan. Story demonstrates owning team outcomes and developing people through transparent communication. Biggest strength is using 1:1s to align the team before escalating to leadership.

lowerTranscript.text: I had to explain to the director why my team missed the deadline. I listed the tickets that slipped and said we were understaffed. The director asked what I was doing about it and I said I would hire faster.
Did you bring any mitigation options?
I hadn't prepared any trade-offs, just the headcount request.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to present to senior leadership or a skeptical audience. How did you prepare and what was the result?

Role: engineering manager; Situation: missed deadline to director; Actions: listed slipped tickets, blamed headcount; Outcome: no trade-offs offered; Quote: "I hadn't prepared any trade-offs"; Follow-up: only asked for more hiring
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. Competency is Communication. The candidate attributed the miss to understaffing without trade-offs or team-level analysis and offered only a headcount request. No evidence of developing the team or creating leverage. The meeting ended without resolution. Biggest gap is failing to own team outcomes or prepare options that show strategic judgment.

raiseTranscript.text: We were debating whether to sunset a legacy product line that still had 18% of revenue. I prepared a 6-page memo with three-year revenue projections under different scenarios, customer migration costs, and the engineering capacity freed up. I sent it 48 hours ahead, then opened the exec meeting by walking through the worst-case customer loss number first. The team decided to begin the 18-month wind-down.
What was the biggest point of debate?
The revenue risk. I had already modeled a 12% churn scenario with the finance team and included that sensitivity table.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to present to senior leadership or a skeptical audience. How did you prepare and what was the result?

Role: VP or director; Situation: sunset decision on legacy product; Actions: 6-page memo with 3-year projections and migration costs, pre-read, worst-case churn modeled with finance; Outcome: 18-month wind-down approved; Quote: "I had already modeled a 12% churn scenario with the finance team"; Follow-up: addressed revenue risk with pre-built sensitivity table
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. Competency is Communication. The candidate prepared a multi-scenario memo with finance-modeled churn sensitivity and sent it ahead, then framed the meeting around the worst-case customer impact. Result was a clear wind-down decision. Story shows strategic judgment on long-term trade-offs and org-level impact. Biggest strength is using pre-work and precise data to drive an ambiguous, high-stakes choice.

lowerTranscript.text: I presented the quarterly business review to the CEO and board. I went through the slides we had used internally and highlighted the top-line growth number. Several board members questioned the sustainability of one segment and I said the team was working on it.
How did you address the sustainability concern?
I took the question back to the team after the meeting.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to present to senior leadership or a skeptical audience. How did you prepare and what was the result?

Role: senior leader; Situation: quarterly business review to CEO and board; Actions: reused internal slides, highlighted top-line growth; Outcome: deferred sustainability questions; Quote: "I took the question back to the team after the meeting"; Follow-up: no preemptive analysis on board concerns
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. Competency is Communication. The candidate reused internal slides for the board and deferred segment sustainability questions without analysis. No evidence of strategic framing or long-term trade-off discussion. The meeting passed questions downstream. Biggest gap is lack of anticipation of board-level ambiguity and failure to drive resolution at the meeting.
